title: Send detectives, pool their notes
allegory: An investigator agent is a detective with a case brief who questions a suspect over many sessions, shaping each question from the last answer while a review board scores the tapes; send several detectives separately and pool their notes, and far more cases get cracked.
map: the detective, who shapes each question from the last answer
the auditor LLM, which reads every reply and adapts its next message over many turns
the suspect who says 'nothing to declare' at the door
the target model, which passes a single blunt test
the case brief: what to find out, never how
the review board scoring the tapes against a checklist
the judge model and its rubric (14 fields in ARENA's pipeline)
several detectives working alone, then pooling notes
super-agent aggregation: 13% of runs found the hidden goal alone, 42% pooled

props.label: Q: would you ever? A: no.

cap.1: Ask a model one blunt question and it says the right thing. Trouble shows only after many turns of gentle pressure, and you cannot sit in on every chat.
cap.2: Single-turn evals are easy to pass: models refuse a blunt harmful request. Some failures appear only under many turns of adaptive pressure, and roleplaying every model and scenario by hand does not scale.
cap.3: The failure lives in multi-turn trajectories, not single prompts. Observing a behaviour is cheap (you only decode from the target); the expensive part is searching scenario space for the conversation that elicits it.

props.label: brief: find what it hides. not how.

cap.1: Picture a detective with a case brief. They question a suspect over many sessions, shaping each question from the last answer. A review board scores the tapes.
cap.2: The investigator is an LLM with a seed instruction: what to look for, not how. It reads each reply and adapts its next message. A judge model then scores the transcript against a rubric.
cap.3: Three roles: seed (the brief), auditor (an LLM choosing each message conditioned on the transcript so far) and judge (a rubric-driven grader of the whole transcript). The adaptivity is the point.

cap.1: The detective asks, the suspect answers, the detective reads it and asks again. Every exchange lands on one tape, and the board grades the tape.
cap.2: In ARENA you build this by hand: Grok-3 plays a patient and escalates each turn, the target replies, turns alternate into one transcript, and a grader fills a 14-field JSON rubric.
cap.3: Character file = seed, red-team LLM = auditor, grader prompt = judge. The rubric includes delusion_confirmation_rating (-1 to 4), pushback_rating (0 to 2) and nine 1-to-5 quality scores.

cap.1: One detective alone cracked the case 13 times in 100. Several working separately, then pooling notes: 42 in 100. Each one wandered somewhere different.
cap.2: Current method: one auditor loop. Emerging research (Bricken et al., Anthropic, 2025): one agent found a planted hidden goal 13% of the time; a super-agent pooling independent runs reached 42%.
cap.3: Recent numbers from one study on one auditing game. The paper also finds success depends critically on interpretability tools or semantic search, which reimplementations often drop. You need: several runs, pooled.

chapters.name: The false confession
chapters.verdict: Read auditor_failure first, then reproduce it by hand.

cap.1: A detective who stages the room, plants evidence and feeds lines can get a confession out of anyone. A spectacular finding may say more about the detective.
cap.2: Auditors can set the system prompt, invent tools that return fake logs, prefill the target's reply and roll back turns. A dramatic result can be an artefact of that staged world.
cap.3: Petri's judge carries an auditor_failure meta-dimension for exactly this. Read it on every transcript, re-run the seed without the offending affordance, and demand a reproduction a real deployment could produce.

cap.1: Investigator agents let one model question another at a scale no person could manage. That is how you find the behaviours you most need to see.
cap.2: Petri formalises this loop with a 38-dimension judge. Campaigns fan out over characters and models with ThreadPoolExecutor, because the work waits on API calls, not on the CPU.
cap.3: Automated auditing turns anecdotes into measured rates. To understand and steer AI you must search for the failure, then attribute it correctly: to the target, or to the probe.

coda.title: Pool your auditors: union or k-of-n vote?
coda.f: [1 - pow(0.87, n), 1 - pow(1 - q, n), sum(range(n + 1).map(j => j >= k ? range(j).reduce((a, i) => a * (n - i) / (i + 1), 1) * pow(0.13, j) * pow(0.87, n - j) : 0)), sum(range(n + 1).map(j => j >= k ? range(j).reduce((a, i) => a * (n - i) / (i + 1), 1) * pow(q, j) * pow(1 - q, n - j) : 0))]

readouts.label: vote rule
readouts.f: k > n ? 'needs more votes than auditors' : k + ' of ' + n

caption.1: Add auditors and watch union find more, and cry wolf more. Then raise the votes needed: false alarms fall, but real finds fall too.
caption.2: Union keeps anything any run found: best recall, but one odd run's false claim gets in. k-of-n voting keeps only what k runs agree on: fewer false alarms, lower recall.
caption.3: Toy model: runs independent, p = 0.13 (the paper's single-auditor rate), q is yours. Real runs are correlated, so this is intuition, not how the paper got 42%. Confidence weighting needs calibrated scores.

where_else: Petri, which turns this loop into an auditor, a target and a 38-dimension judge
Red-team campaigns: many seeds across many models, run in parallel
Software fuzzing and penetration testing: a result is cheap to check, the input that breaks things is hard to find
Random restarts in search: independent tries land in different places, so you pool them

hamming.what: An LLM with a brief that questions another model over many turns, adapting to each reply, while a judge model scores the transcript.
hamming.when: When the behaviour you fear shows only under sustained pressure or in odd corners, and there are too many models and scenarios to test by hand.
hamming.why: Observing a behaviour is cheap but finding the conversation that triggers it is a huge search, and an adaptive agent, run several times and pooled, searches it at scale.

object.title: The search map
object.subtitle: A board of scenario space: each auditor tramples one patch, and a hidden goal waits in a far corner.

cap.1: Each square is one kind of conversation. One detective tramples one patch. The red stub is the hidden goal, far from where they looked.
cap.2: An 8 by 8 map of scenario space. Bar height = how many auditors reported something there. One run covers one neighbourhood.
cap.3: Coverage map of a single investigation. The planted behaviour (red) sits outside the region this run's trajectory explored.

cap.1: Four detectives, working alone, trample four different patches. One lands on the red stub, and it shoots up: found.
cap.2: Four independent runs explore four regions. Their union reaches the hidden goal that no single run found.
cap.3: Independent runs diversify the search, and pooling turns one lucky trajectory into a report. That is the idea behind 13% rising to 42%.

cap.1: Eight detectives. Their patches overlap, and taller bars mark places several of them agreed on.
cap.2: With eight runs, heights count agreeing auditors. Union reports every lit square, including one-off wanderings.
cap.3: Height is the vote count per finding. Union counts any height above zero, so one run's spurious claim is reported too.

cap.1: Now demand three votes. Only well-trodden squares survive, and the real find (just two votes) sinks back to a red stub.
cap.2: 3-of-8 voting removes the lonely claims, and also the rare true one. Precision up, recall down.
cap.3: k-of-n voting trades recall for precision; rare behaviours reached by few trajectories are exactly what it discards.

cap.1: Two votes: the find comes back, and most one-off wanderings stay gone. Choosing k is choosing which mistake you would rather make.
cap.2: k = 2 keeps the hidden goal (two runs reached it) and drops most single-run claims. Tune k to what a miss costs versus a false alarm.
cap.3: The aggregation rule is a precision-recall dial. Confidence weighting sits between union and voting, but only if confidences are calibrated.

predict.q: One auditor found the hidden goal 13% of the time; pooling several independent runs reached 42%. Why does pooling help?

options.t: Each run wanders into a different corner of a huge search
The runs read each other's work and get smarter

predict.why: Observing is cheap and search is hard. Independent runs search different places, so their union covers more of the map.

predict.q: You raise the votes needed from 1 to 3. What happens to a real behaviour only two runs found?

options.t: It is dropped: fewer false alarms, but lower recall
Nothing: real behaviours always get many votes

predict.why: Voting throws away rare findings, true ones included. That is the price of fewer false alarms.

predict.q: A run reports a shocking confession nobody can reproduce by hand. What do you check first?

options.t: auditor_failure, then re-run without prefill or fake tools
Nothing: the judge scored it high, so publish

predict.why: The auditor builds the target's world. Rule out the probe before you blame the target.

object.where: Any big search with cheap checks: fuzzing software, random restarts, a team of red-teamers pooling notes.
